findings.failure_scenario: register_shipment_events('sent') followed later by register_shipment_events('delivered') returns {'delivered': ['sent', 'delivered']}, misreporting which events belong to the current type.

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: load_order_rows builds the SQL statement by interpolating owner_id directly into an f-string and executes it. The owner_id value is attacker-controllable through whatever calls this helper, so it can break out of the string literal and run arbitrary SQL. Use a parameterized query instead.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies an owner_id like `' OR '1'='1` or `'; DROP TABLE orders; --`, the interpolated query executes with that payload, exposing or modifying orders for all customers.
findings.suggestion:
query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = %s"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
findings.title: SQL injection via f-string query construction

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: register_shipment_events defaults events to a shared list literal. The same list object is reused across every call that omits the argument, and events.append mutates it, so unrelated invocations accumulate each other's event types. The returned dictionary then reports events from previous calls. Use None and create a fresh list per call.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling register_shipment_events('shipped') then register_shipment_events('returned') returns {'returned': ['shipped', 'returned']} instead of only the new event, corrupting downstream event records.
findings.title: Mutable default argument leaks state across calls

findings.body: The loop starts at range(1, len(entries)), so entries[0] is never scored or returned. Every caller loses the first invoice entry regardless of its score. Start the range at 0.
findings.failure_scenario: An invoice batch whose first entry has the highest score is ranked without it, so the top entry disappears from the ranked output and downstream billing omits it.
findings.suggestion: for position in range(len(entries)):
findings.title: rank_invoice_entries silently drops the first entry

findings.body: The docstring promises constant-time selection assuming chronological arrival, but the implementation sorts the whole list by created_at, which is O(n log n) and discards the arrival-order assumption. If records are already chronological, return the last element directly; otherwise the docstring is misleading.
findings.failure_scenario: Large queue record sets pay an unnecessary full sort on every call, and callers trusting the constant-time contract may invoke it in hot paths where it becomes a latency bottleneck.
findings.title: newest_queue_id sorts despite constant-time claim

findings.body: datetime.datetime.utcnow() is deprecated in modern Python and produces a naive datetime. Use datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc) so created_at is timezone-aware and unambiguous.
findings.failure_scenario: Naive UTC stamps can be misinterpreted or fail when compared with timezone-aware timestamps elsewhere in the pipeline.
findings.suggestion: stamp = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat()
findings.title: Use timezone-aware UTC timestamps

findings.body: The function accepts a threshold argument but hardcodes 5000 in the comparison, so callers cannot control the review cutoff and the parameter is silently ignored. Compare against the passed threshold.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passing threshold=1000 to catch smaller backorders still only sees rows above 5000 flagged, silently missing reviews the caller expected.
findings.suggestion: if float(row["total"]) > threshold:
findings.title: flag_large_backorder_totals ignores its threshold parameter

findings.anchor: def newest_queue_id(records: list[dict[str, object]]) -> str | None:
findings.body: newest_queue_id's docstring says it returns the newest identifier in constant time, but the implementation calls sorted(records, ...), which is O(n log n) and also allocates a full sorted copy.
findings.suggestion:
"""Return the newest queue identifier.

    Assumes records arrive in chronological order.
    """
findings.title: Docstring claims constant time but implementation sorts

findings.body: seen is a list and membership is tested with `label in seen`, which scans the list linearly. The whole function becomes O(n²) in the number of rows; a set gives O(1) membership checks.
findings.failure_scenario: With a large batch of payment rows, each new label triggers a scan of all previously seen labels, making deduplication increasingly slow as the input grows.
findings.suggestion: seen: set[str] = set()
findings.title: Use a set for duplicate-label lookups

findings.body: The inner double loop recomputes the same zone × weight viability count for every carrier even though the count does not depend on the carrier. The work is O(carriers × zones × weights); computing the count once and reusing it is O(zones × weights + carriers).
findings.failure_scenario: With large zone, weight, and carrier lists, the function performs the identical nested scan once per carrier, multiplying runtime by the number of carriers unnecessarily.
findings.suggestion:
count = sum(1 for zone in zones for weight in weights if weight > 0 and zone)
    return {carrier: count for carrier in carriers}
findings.title: Nested zone/weight scan repeats per carrier

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: owner_id is interpolated directly into the SQL string with an f-string before cursor.execute. This allows SQL injection and can also break the query if owner_id contains a quote. Use a bound parameter; the exact placeholder style depends on the DB-API driver in use.
findings.failure_scenario: If owner_id is controlled or influenced by external input, a value such as "x' OR '1'='1" alters the WHERE clause, causing the query to return or expose order rows belonging to other customers.
findings.suggestion:
query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = %s"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
findings.title: Parameterize the SQL query instead of interpolating owner_id

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: The default events=[] is created once at function definition and shared by every call that omits events. Appending to it makes event history leak across calls, so later invocations return events recorded by earlier unrelated calls.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling register_shipment_events("created") and then register_shipment_events("shipped") without passing events returns {"shipped": ["created", "shipped"]} on the second call because both calls mutate the same shared list.
findings.title: Avoid a mutable default argument in register_shipment_events

findings.body: The loop starts at range(1, len(entries)), so entries[0] is never scored or returned. The docstring says entries are ranked by score, but the first element is silently dropped.

findings.suggestion:

findings.failure_scenario: If created_at values are later compared with timezone-aware timestamps, the naive UTC string can be parsed or interpreted inconsistently, producing incorrect ordering of manifest checkpoints.
findings.suggestion: stamp = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat()
findings.title: Use timezone-aware UTC time instead of datetime.utcnow()

findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes threshold=1000 expecting lower-value rows to be flagged; the function still only flags totals above 5000, silently ignoring the argument.
findings.suggestion: if float(row["total"]) > threshold:

findings.anchor: def newest_queue_id(records: list[dict[str, object]]) -> str | None:
findings.body: The docstring claims the lookup runs in constant time and assumes chronological arrival, but the implementation sorts all records, which is O(n log n) and ignores arrival order. Either the documented contract or the code is wrong; as written the name/docstring contradicts the behaviour.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller relies on the documented constant-time guarantee for large record lists and sees O(n log n) sorting cost, or relies on the chronological-order assumption while the code re-sorts by created_at strings and returns a different record.

findings.body: The SQL statement is built by interpolating owner_id directly into the query string, so any quotes or SQL syntax in the input become part of the statement. Use a bound parameter with a placeholder instead of string formatting.

findings.body: datetime.utcnow() is deprecated since Python 3.12 and produces a naive datetime string with no offset. The modern replacement is datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc), which returns a timezone-aware value; isoformat() then includes the +00:00 offset.
findings.failure_scenario: When a checkpoint stamped here is later compared or parsed alongside timezone-aware timestamps, the naive UTC string can cause TypeError or silent mis-ordering of checkpoints.
findings.suggestion: stamp = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat()
findings.title: Use timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc)

findings.body: The docstring says the function returns the newest queue identifier in constant time and assumes records arrive in chronological order, but the implementation sorts the entire list, which is O(n log n) and does not rely on input order. The documentation contradicts the changed code.

    """

If skipping the first entry is intentional, the docstring must say so; otherwise the loop bound contradicts the documented behaviour.

findings.title: Document rank_invoice_entries skipping first entry

findings.anchor: """Record shipment events of one type and return the events per type."""
findings.body: register_shipment_events is a new public helper with a mutable default list argument. Its docstring says it records events and returns events per type, but does not explain that state persists across calls through the default argument or that only the current event type is returned. The signature and documented behaviour therefore under-describe the observable side effect.
